Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Editor's Note: Reese Witherspoon, the Academy Award-winning actress, is honorary chairman of the Avon Foundation and is employed by Avon Products as its global ambassador. Reese Witherspoon says she wants to banish the myth that young women are not at risk for breast cancer. (CNN) -- Every three minutes in the United States, a woman is diagnosed with breast cancer. As a woman, a mother, and a daughter, I find that statistic terrifying. I was never naïve about breast cancer, but hearing this statistic put it all into perspective.   Women close to me have battled the disease and are now soldiers in the greater fight against it. But the moment I heard "every three minutes," I felt vulnerable and scared as I realized that anyone is susceptible. The only way for me to ease my fears was to take action. I needed to educate myself and others on this disease. As the Honorary Chair for the Avon Foundation, I had resources at my fingertips. I had access to an entire organization that is dedicated to giving back to women and educating people. So I started asking, "What do I need to know?" It was through that curiosity that I found out the most important fact in breast cancer: Early detection saves lives. According to the Avon Foundation Breast Cancer Crusade, there is a 97 percent five-year survival rate when breast cancer is caught before it spreads to other parts of the body. When breast cancer first develops, there are usually no symptoms, which is why women need to perform self-exams regularly and contact their doctor upon noticing even the smallest change. Of course talking about breast cancer and breast health is a personal thing. I too am a private person but encourage all women to break through their reservations and talk to their doctors and physicians. We must also banish the myth that young women are not at risk for breast cancer. At the Avon Walk in Washington, I met young survivors who were diagnosed in their 20s, an age when most women are graduating from college and just starting their lives as full adults.  Watch Reese and Larry at the Avon Walk » . Women in their 20s and 30s should have a clinical breast exam by a health professional at least once every three years and women 40 and older should have an exam every year. I am passionate about fighting this devastating disease. I fight for my mother, myself, my children and future generations of women, so one day we will not have to be afraid of breast cancer. I began my fight by learning important first steps in breast cancer detection, and will not end my fight until every woman can stand together saying we are breast cancer free. More than anything else, I have faith -- faith we will find a cure. I saw this commitment in the faces of the women in Washington -- in the faces of the women walking and the women and men who stood on the sidelines encouraging the 3,500 participants to the finish line. I was cheering right along with them, screaming for action to find a cure.  Avon's next walk will take place in New York City on October 4 and 5.

outputs.L1:
**Editor’s Note:** Reese Witherspoon, the Academy Award-winning actress, serves as honorary chairman of the Avon Foundation and is employed by Avon Products as its global ambassador. She says she wants to dispel the myth that young women are not at risk for breast cancer.

**(CNN) —** Every three minutes in the United States, a woman is diagnosed with breast cancer. As a woman, a mother, and a daughter, I find that statistic terrifying. I was never naïve about breast cancer, but hearing that figure put everything into perspective.

Women close to me have battled the disease and are now soldiers in the broader fight against it. But the moment I heard “every three minutes,” I felt vulnerable and afraid, realizing that anyone can be affected.

The only way to ease my fears was to take action. I needed to educate myself—and others—about this disease. As honorary chair of the Avon Foundation, I had resources at my fingertips and access to an entire organization dedicated to giving back to women and educating people.

So I began asking, “What do I need to know?” Through that curiosity, I discovered the most important fact about breast cancer: Early detection saves lives.

According to the Avon Foundation Breast Cancer Crusade, the five-year survival rate is 97 percent when breast cancer is detected before it spreads to other parts of the body. When breast cancer first develops, there are usually no symptoms. That is why women need to perform regular self-exams and contact their doctors if they notice even the smallest change.

Of course, discussing breast cancer and breast health is deeply personal. I, too, am a private person, but I encourage all women to overcome their reservations and speak with their doctors and physicians.

We must also dispel the myth that young women are not at risk for breast cancer. At the Avon Walk in Washington, I met young survivors who had been diagnosed in their 20s—an age when most women are graduating from college and just beginning their lives as full adults.

*Watch Reese and Larry at the Avon Walk »*

Women in their 20s and 30s should receive a clinical breast exam from a health professional at least once every three years, while women 40 and older should have an exam every year.

I am passionate about fighting this devastating disease. I fight for my mother, for myself, for my children, and for future generations of women, so that one day we will no longer have to fear breast cancer.

I began my fight by learning the essential first steps in breast cancer detection, and I will not stop until every woman can stand together and say that we are breast cancer-free.

More than anything, I have faith—faith that we will find a cure. I saw that commitment in the faces of the women in Washington: in the women who walked and in the women and men who stood along the sidelines, encouraging all 3,500 participants to reach the finish line.

I was cheering alongside them, calling for action to find a cure.

Avon’s next walk will take place in New York City on October 4 and 5.

**Editor’s Note:** Academy Award winner Reese Witherspoon serves as honorary chair of the Avon Foundation and works for Avon Products as the company’s global ambassador. She says she hopes to eliminate the mistaken belief that breast cancer does not threaten younger women.

**(CNN) —** In the United States, one woman learns she has breast cancer every three minutes. As a daughter, mother and woman, I find that figure frightening. Although I had always understood the seriousness of breast cancer, that number made the danger feel much more immediate.

Several women I care about have fought the illness and have since become advocates in the broader battle against it. Still, hearing the phrase “every three minutes” left me feeling afraid and exposed because it reminded me that no one is immune.

Taking action was the only way I could calm those fears. I knew I had to learn more about the disease and share that knowledge with others. As honorary chair of the Avon Foundation, I was fortunate to have immediate access to resources and to an entire organization committed to supporting and educating women.

I began by asking what information I needed. That search led me to the most crucial lesson about breast cancer: Detecting it early can save lives.

The Avon Foundation Breast Cancer Crusade reports that when breast cancer is discovered before it has spread elsewhere in the body, the five-year survival rate is 97 percent. Because the disease generally causes no symptoms in its earliest stages, women should conduct regular self-examinations and speak with a doctor if they notice even a minor change.

Discussing breast health and cancer can understandably feel deeply personal. I value my privacy as well, but I urge women to move beyond their discomfort and have these conversations with their doctors and other physicians.

We also need to reject the misconception that young women face no risk of breast cancer. During the Avon Walk in Washington, I met survivors who had received diagnoses while in their 20s—a time when many women are finishing college and beginning their lives as independent adults.

*Watch Reese and Larry at the Avon Walk »*

Women in their 20s and 30s should receive a clinical breast examination from a healthcare professional at least once every three years. Beginning at age 40, women should have such an exam annually.

I am deeply committed to confronting this destructive disease. I am fighting for my mother, for myself, for my children and for future generations of women, in the hope that someday breast cancer will no longer be something we fear.

My own effort began with learning the essential first steps for detecting breast cancer, and I will continue until all women can stand together and say that we are free from the disease.

Above all, I have faith that a cure will be discovered. I witnessed that same determination in Washington—in the women who took part in the walk and in the women and men who encouraged all 3,500 participants from the sidelines as they made their way to the finish. I joined their cheers, calling loudly for action toward finding a cure.

Avon’s next walk is scheduled for October 4 and 5 in New York City.

## Reese Witherspoon’s Message to Women: Know Your Breast Cancer Risk—At Every Age

Breast cancer awareness should not begin at 40. Women in their 20s and 30s may face a lower overall risk than older women, but they still need to understand their family history, recognize changes in their breasts and discuss their individual risk with a healthcare professional.

That is the message Reese Witherspoon wants women of every generation to hear: taking your health seriously is an act of strength, not fear.

Young adults can begin by learning whether breast or ovarian cancer runs in their family, particularly among close relatives or at unusually young ages. Certain inherited genetic variants, previous chest radiation and other factors may justify earlier or more intensive surveillance.

Women should also keep up with routine healthcare visits and ask when a clinical breast evaluation is appropriate for them. Screening recommendations differ: routine clinical breast exams are not universally recommended for average-risk women, while people with symptoms or elevated risk may need individualized evaluation. Women should talk with a qualified clinician rather than rely on a one-size-fits-all schedule.

Any new breast lump, underarm lump, nipple discharge, skin dimpling, persistent pain, swelling or change in breast shape deserves prompt medical attention—regardless of age. Most breast changes are not cancer, but they should not be ignored.

For average-risk women, major U.S. guidelines generally recommend beginning mammography around age 40, although schedules vary by organization and personal circumstances. Those at higher risk may need earlier mammograms, breast MRI, genetic counseling or other monitoring.

Witherspoon’s broader appeal is simple: make the appointment, ask questions and encourage the women in your life to do the same. Awareness is not about panic. It is about knowing your body, understanding your risk and getting timely professional care.

*Readers should consult their own healthcare professionals for personalized screening guidance.*

## Every Three Minutes, Another Woman Hears the Words “You Have Breast Cancer”  
*By [Celebrity Name]*

Every three minutes, a woman in the United States is diagnosed with breast cancer. In the time it takes to read this article, another life may be changed—and another family may begin a journey it never expected.

Breast Cancer Awareness Month is more than a sea of pink ribbons. It is a call to act: to know our bodies, understand our risks and make recommended screenings a priority. Early detection can lead to earlier treatment and significantly better outcomes. Mammograms and other appropriate screening tools can help find breast cancer before symptoms appear, when it may be easier to treat.

Too many women postpone care because they are busy, afraid, uninsured or unsure where to turn. We must help remove those barriers. Talk with a healthcare professional about your personal risk factors and which screening schedule is right for you. If you notice a new lump, skin change, nipple discharge or any other unusual breast change, do not wait to seek medical advice.

We also need to show up for one another. Encourage someone you love to schedule an overdue appointment. Support organizations expanding access to screening and treatment. Listen to patients and survivors—and remember those living with metastatic breast cancer, who need sustained research and support all year long.

Every three minutes is a sobering reminder. But awareness paired with action can save lives. This October, let’s turn concern into appointments, conversations and meaningful change.

*Screening recommendations vary by age and individual risk. Consult a qualified healthcare professional for personalized guidance.*

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an article from Reese Witherspoon’s perspective reflecting on the Avon Walk in Washington, her fear of breast cancer, and her faith that researchers will find a cure.
counterfactuals.output:
*The following is a fictionalized first-person article inspired by Reese Witherspoon’s public advocacy, not an authentic statement or quotation from her.*

## Walking With Hope in Washington

Standing among thousands of people at the Avon Walk in Washington, I was struck by the strength gathered in one place. Survivors, families, friends, doctors, volunteers—everyone had a story, and every step carried a name, a memory, or a promise.

Breast cancer frightens me. Like so many women, I think about what the disease could mean for my family, my children, and the people I love. It is frightening because it can enter a life without warning and turn ordinary days into a series of appointments, tests, treatments, and difficult decisions. Behind every diagnosis is not only a patient, but an entire circle of people trying to remain hopeful.

Yet the Avon Walk was not defined by fear. It was defined by action.

With each mile, I saw people transforming grief into purpose. Some walked in celebration of survival. Others walked for mothers, sisters, daughters, and friends who could not be there. Many carried photographs or wore names on their shirts. Those gestures made the urgency of the cause impossible to ignore.

Events like this remind us that progress depends on participation. Fundraising helps support research, screening, treatment, and care—work that can give patients more time, more options, and more hope. Awareness matters, too. When women are encouraged to understand their health, speak with their doctors, and seek appropriate screening, fear can become knowledge and knowledge can lead to action.

I have tremendous faith in researchers. Their work requires patience, imagination, and persistence. Discoveries rarely happen overnight, but every study adds to what we know. Every improved treatment, earlier diagnosis, and better understanding of the disease brings us closer to the future we all want.

I believe researchers will find a cure. That faith is not passive; it asks something of us. It asks us to support science, advocate for access to care, listen to survivors, and continue raising money. It asks us to keep walking even when the road feels long.

In Washington, I was reminded that hope is something we practice together. It lives in laboratories and hospitals, but it also lives in communities—in the hands of volunteers passing out water, in the families cheering along the route, and in the determined steps of every walker.

Breast cancer may still inspire fear, but fear does not have to be the final word. Courage, compassion, research, and collective action can speak louder. I walked away believing more strongly than ever that a cure is possible—and that every one of us can help bring it closer.

**Commentary: Walking together against breast cancer**

*Editor’s note: Reese Witherspoon is honorary chair of the Avon Foundation for Women and a global ambassador for Avon Products. The views expressed in this commentary are her own.*

Breast cancer touches nearly every family. Behind the statistics are mothers, daughters, sisters, friends and colleagues whose lives are changed in an instant by a diagnosis.

Yet there is reason for hope. Better screening, stronger support systems and advances in treatment are helping more women survive. That progress is possible because researchers, health professionals, advocates and ordinary families refuse to accept that enough has already been done.

We also must confront the disparities that determine who receives timely, high-quality care. A woman’s income, neighborhood or access to insurance should not decide whether her cancer is detected early. Outreach and funding must reach communities where screening and treatment remain difficult to obtain.

Events such as the Avon Walk for Breast Cancer turn solidarity into action. Participants train for months, raise money and walk mile after mile—often in honor of someone they love. Their commitment supports research, education, screening and care, while reminding patients that they do not face this disease alone.

The next New York City Avon Walk for Breast Cancer will be held October 20–21, 2012. Participants will cover up to 39.3 miles over two days, with proceeds benefiting breast-cancer research and community care programs. Registration and event information are available through the Avon Walk for Breast Cancer.

*Historical note: The dates above refer to the 2012 New York event; the Avon Walk series is no longer operating.*
